newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel rejects any previous "deals" on Golan.
newsitem.headline: Israel rejects any previous "deals" on Golan.

text.p: Israel's right-wing government said on Thursday it would not be held to what it described as an "indirect" agreement by assassinated Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin for a complete Israeli pullout from the Golan Heights.
Israel's former chief negotiator with Syria and a top Rabin aide have denied the late Israeli leader made any commitment for a total withdrawal from the northern plateau.
After its weekly meeting, the cabinet released a statement quoting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as confirming the accuracy of Israeli newspaper reports about a Rabin commitment on withdrawal.
But it said Netanyahu acknowledged there had been no written promise.

"(Netanyahu) said...newspaper reports that the late prime minister, Yitzhak Rabin, agreed indirectly to withdraw from the Golan Heights to the June 4, 1967 lines -- on condition that Syria met a number of conditions -- and that his agreement was passed on to the United States, are correct," it said.

"The position accepted by the U.S. administration today is that hypothetical statements made by the previous government during negotiations are not binding on the current Israeli government," the statement said.

By asserting the accuracy of the reports about Rabin, Netanyahu also appeared to be trying to score political points against former Labour Prime Minister Shimon Peres, whom he defeated in last May's general election.

The reports, based on a new book about Rabin by political reporter Orly Azulai-Katz, said Peres had been kept out of the decision loop and had been stunned to learn about the tacit agreement on taking office after Rabin was killed.

Commenting on the purported agreement for a full pullout, Itamar Rabinovich, Israel's former chief negotiator with Syria, said on Wednesday: "Yitzhak Rabin did not promise or commit to withdraw from the Golan."
Eitan Haber, a top Rabin aide, said: "To the best of my knowledge, there was never anything like this."
Syria said on Thursday it would not agree to fresh talks with Israel until Netanyahu accepted all the understandings reached with the Jewish state's previous government.

"Netanyahu is ready to negotiate without committing himself to withdrawal from the Golan. The previous agreements and understandings do not bind his government. He doesn't want to resume the talks from the point where they stopped but from the zero point," the official daily al-Thawra newspaper said.
Syria has maintained in five years of sporadic talks that only a full Israel withdrawal from the Golan Heights captured in the 1967 Middle East war would lead to peace.
Netanyahu wants to keep the Golan in Israeli hands and has called on Syria to renew talks unconditionally.
Peres and Rabin had agreed in talks with Arab partners to the principle of exchanging land for peace but said the extent of Israel's withdrawal depended on Syria's readiness for normalisation.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Wednesday after talks between Netanyahu and U.S. leaders that Washington and Israel had developed proposals for restarting peace talks with Syria, suspended since March.
Burns said U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross had long talks on the subject with Dore Gold, a key adviser to Netanyahu, after the Israeli leader met President Bill Clinton on Monday.
Ross may travel to the Middle East next week, U.S. officials said.
